The '''67th Academy Awards''' ceremony, organized by the [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] (AMPAS) took place on March 27, 1995, at the [[Shrine Auditorium]] in [[Los Angeles]] beginning at 6:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Pacific Time Zone|PST]] / 9:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Eastern Time Zone|EST]]. During the ceremony, AMPAS presented Academy Awards (commonly referred to as the Oscars) in 23 categories honoring the [[1994 in film|films released in 1994]]. The ceremony, televised in the United States by [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]], was produced by [[Gilbert Cates]] and directed by [[Jeff Margolis]].<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=87}}</ref> Comedian [[David Letterman]] hosted the show for the first time.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Archerd |first1=Army |title=Letterman to skip bowling, host Oscars |url=https://variety.com/1995/voices/columns/letterman-to-skip-bowling-host-oscars-1117862616/ |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=Variety  |date=January 12, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714212353/http://variety.com/1995/voices/columns/letterman-to-skip-bowling-host-oscars-1117862616/ |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref> Three weeks earlier in a ceremony held at the [[Beverly Wilshire Hotel|Regent Beverly Wilshire Hotel]] in [[Beverly Hills, California]] on March 4, the [[Academy Award for Technical Achievement|Academy Awards for Technical Achievement]] were presented by host [[Jamie Lee Curtis]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Past Scientific & Technical Awards Ceremonies|url=http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|access-date=July 31, 2013|work=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]]|publisher=AMPAS|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140213185729/http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|archive-date=February 13, 2014}}</ref>

''[[Forrest Gump]]'' won six awards, including [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Grimes |first1=William |title='Forrest Gump' Triumphs With 6 Academy Awards |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/03/28/movies/forrest-gump-triumphs-with-6-academy-awards.html |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=The New York Times  |date=March 28, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140810175320/http://www.nytimes.com/1995/03/28/movies/forrest-gump-triumphs-with-6-academy-awards.html |archive-date=August 10, 2014 }}</ref> Other winners included ''[[Ed Wood (film)|Ed Wood]]'', ''[[The Lion King]]'', and ''[[Speed (1994 film)|Speed]]'' with two awards and ''[[The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert]]''; ''[[Blue Sky (1994 film)|Blue Sky]]'', ''[[Bob's Birthday]]'', ''[[Bullets Over Broadway]]'', ''[[Burnt by the Sun]]'', ''[[Franz Kafka's It's a Wonderful Life]]'', ''[[Legends of the Fall]]'', ''[[The Madness of King George]]'', ''[[Maya Lin: A Strong Clear Vision]]'', ''[[Pulp Fiction]]'', ''[[A Time for Justice]]'', and ''[[Trevor (film)|Trevor]]'' with one. The telecast garnered more than 48 million viewers in the United States, making it the most watched Oscars telecast since the [[55th Academy Awards]] in 1983.

==Winners and nominees==
<!-- Please do not add any fact or statement below unless you have a credible source verifying it. Otherwise, it will be promptly removed. -->

The nominees for the 67th Academy Awards were announced on February 14, 1995, at the [[Samuel Goldwyn Theater]] in [[Beverly Hills, California]], by [[Arthur Hiller]], the then-president of the Academy, and actress [[Angela Bassett]].<ref>{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=963}}</ref> ''[[Forrest Gump]]'' earned the most nominations with thirteen. It was the most nominated film since 1966's ''[[Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (film)|Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?]]'' and the fifth film to earn that many nominations.<ref>{{cite news |title=Acad Sees The 'Forrest' For The Oscars |url=https://variety.com/1995/film/features/acad-sees-the-forrest-for-the-oscars-99124576/ |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=Variety |date=February 15, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714222756/http://variety.com/1995/film/features/acad-sees-the-forrest-for-the-oscars-99124576/ |archive-date=July 14, 2014}}</ref> ''[[Bullets Over Broadway]]'', ''[[Pulp Fiction]]'', and ''[[The Shawshank Redemption]]'' tied for second with seven each.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Boyar |first1=Jay |title=The Oscar Nominations |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1995/02/15/the-oscar-nominations-2/ |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=Orlando Sentinel |date=February 15, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714145645/http://articles.orlandosentinel.com/1995-02-15/lifestyle/9502140419_1_forrest-gump-nominations-hoop-dreams |archive-date=July 14, 2014}}</ref>

The winners were announced during the awards ceremony on March 27, 1995. ''Forrest Gump'' was the highest grossing [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]] winner in history.<ref name="LAT"/> For only the second time in Oscar history, three of the four acting winners were previous winners. The [[11th Academy Awards|11th ceremony]] held in 1939 previously accomplished this feat.<ref>{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=986}}</ref> Best Actor winner [[Tom Hanks]] became the fifth performer to win consecutive acting Oscars and the second person to do so in the aforementioned category since [[Spencer Tracy]] won for his performances in ''[[Captains Courageous (1937 film)|Captains Courageous]]'' (1937) and ''[[Boys Town (film)|Boys Town]]'' (1938).<ref>{{harvnb|Osborne|2013|p=423}}</ref><ref name="LAT">{{cite news |last1=Eller |first1=Claudia |title=It's a Sweet Evening for 'Gump' With 6 Awards : Movies: Film earns best director for Zemeckis and another best actor honor for Hanks. Lange also wins. |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1995-03-28-mn-48102-story.html |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 28, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714231015/http://articles.latimes.com/1995-03-28/news/mn-48102_1_robert-zemeckis |archive-date=July 14, 2014}}</ref> He also was the sixth person to win Best Actor twice.<ref>{{cite news |last1=O'Neil |first1=Tom |title=Day-Lewis is 8th double Oscar lead actor |url=http://goldderby.latimes.com/awards_goldderby/2008/02/day-lewis-is-8t.html |access-date=April 11, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=February 24, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140715033349/http://goldderby.latimes.com/awards_goldderby/2008/02/day-lewis-is-8t.html |archive-date=July 15, 2014}}</ref> Best Supporting Actress winner [[Dianne Wiest]] became the first person to win two acting Oscars for performances in films directed by the same person.{{refn|group=lower-alpha|[[Walter Brennan]]'s first Oscar-winning role in ''[[Come and Get It (1936 film)|Come and Get It]]'' (1936) was partially directed by [[William Wyler]], the same director who helmed his third winning role in ''[[The Westerner (1940 film)|The Westerner]]'' (1940). (Brennan's second win for ''[[Kentucky (film)|Kentucky]]'' (1938) had no connection to Wyler.) However, Wyler was coerced into finishing ''Come and Get It'' after producer [[Samuel Goldwyn]] fired original director, [[Howard Hawks]]—who completed two-thirds of the film, albeit after significantly modifying the adaptation of [[Edna Ferber]]'s original story. Wyler reluctantly allowed his name to have shared credit, but later disowned the film from his filmography. Otherwise, Brennan would have been the first to claim this laurel, technically.}} She first won in that same category for her role in [[Woody Allen]]'s 1986 film ''[[Hannah and Her Sisters]]''.<ref>{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=1181}}</ref> ''[[Franz Kafka's It's a Wonderful Life]]'' and ''[[Trevor (film)|Trevor]]''{{'}}s joint win in the Best Live Action Short category marked the fifth occurrence of a tie in Oscar history; the next tie would occur at the [[85th Academy Awards]] in 2013.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Warner |first1=Denise |title=Best Sound Editing Oscar tie is sixth in Academy Awards history |url=http://insidemovies.ew.com/2013/02/24/sound-editing-tie-oscars/ |access-date=July 8, 2014 |magazine=Entertainment Weekly |date=February 24, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140331161848/http://insidemovies.ew.com/2013/02/24/sound-editing-tie-oscars/ |archive-date=March 31, 2014}}</ref>

==Ceremony information==
Despite earning critical praise for the [[66th Academy Awards|previous year's ceremony]], actress and comedian [[Whoopi Goldberg]] announced that she would not host the ceremony for a second consecutive year saying, "I've had a great time, but I've done it."<ref>{{cite magazine|last1=Broeske |first1=Pat H. |title=Leader of the Pack |url=http://www.ew.com/article/1994/12/23/whoopi-goldbergs-one-time-host |access-date=July 8, 2014 |magazine=Entertainment Weekly  |date=December 23, 1994 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714193548/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0%2C%2C305005%2C00.html |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref> She added that her role in the upcoming movie ''[[Bogus (film)|Bogus]]'' would jeopardize her busy schedule.<ref name="No Goldberg or Crystal">{{cite news|last1=Dutka |first1=Elaine |title=No Crystal Ball at Oscars Again |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1995-01-07-ca-17206-story.html |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times  |date=January 7, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714213803/http://articles.latimes.com/1995-01-07/entertainment/ca-17206_1_oscars-crystal-ball |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref> In addition, her [[Comic Relief USA|Comic Relief]] co-host and veteran Oscar emcee [[Billy Crystal]] declined to host the show citing his commitment to his film ''[[Forget Paris]]'' which he directed, wrote, starred in, and produced.<ref name="No Goldberg or Crystal" /> Producer Gil Cates hired actor, comedian, and ''[[Late Show with David Letterman|Late Show]]'' host [[David Letterman]] as host of the 1995 ceremony.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Carter |first1=Bill |title=Letterman to Be Oscars Show Host |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/01/13/movies/letterman-to-be-oscars-show-host.html |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=The New York Times  |date=January 13, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140716121410/http://www.nytimes.com/1995/01/13/movies/letterman-to-be-oscars-show-host.html |archive-date=July 16, 2014 }}</ref> Cates explained his decision to hire the late-night talk show host saying, "He's punctual, he's well groomed, and he knows how to keep an audience awake."<ref name="Comedy">{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=967}}</ref> [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] entertainment president [[Ted Harbert]] also approved of the choice stating, "If Dave likes the experience, this could be a great answer for the show, just the way [[Johnny Carson]] did the show for many years."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Carroll |first1=Jerry |title=The Dave and Oscar Show: Will Letterman's acid humor take the mush out of the Academy Awards? |url=http://www.sfgate.com/entertainment/article/THE-DAVE-AND-OSCAR-SHOW-Will-Letterman-s-acid-3039257.php |access-date=July 9, 2014 |work=San Francisco Chronicle |date=March 26, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714190419/http://www.sfgate.com/entertainment/article/THE-DAVE-AND-OSCAR-SHOW-Will-Letterman-s-acid-3039257.php |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref>

As with previous ceremonies he produced, Cates centered the show on a theme. This year, he christened the show with the theme "Comedy and the Movies" commenting "This year, because of the earthquakes and floods and [[Bosnia]] and [[Rwanda]], it was a (terrible) year, and therefore seemed a great year to celebrate what movies can really give us, which is an opportunity to go for two hours in the dark and laugh together. Even with television, it's not a community experience unless you have a very big family. So it's unique to movies and theater, and it's this very human thing."<ref name="Comedy" /><ref name="Comedy Oscars">{{cite news|last1=Willman |first1=Chris |title=Oscar Show Promises Lots of Funny Business : Awards: Comedy's the theme, from Letterman to Stupid Pet Tricks to film clips loaded with historic laughs. But will it come in under the time limit? |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1995-03-27-ca-47711-story.html |access-date=July 9, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times  |date=March 27, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140715040217/http://articles.latimes.com/1995-03-27/entertainment/ca-47711_1_stupid-pet-trick |archive-date=July 15, 2014 }}</ref> In tandem with the theme, the ceremony's opening number featured a montage produced by [[Chuck Workman]] featuring scenes of humorous moments from a variety of both comedic and non-comedic films projected on a large screen on the stage. During that segment, actors [[Tim Curry]], [[Kathy Najimy]], and [[Mara Wilson]] performed a modified version of the song "[[Make 'Em Laugh]]" from the film ''[[Singin' in the Rain]]'', using [[Chroma key|blue screen]] technology to make it appear that they were jumping in and out of the montage on the screen.<ref>Multiple sources:
*{{cite magazine |last1=Cagle |first1=Jess |title=Chatty Kathy |url=https://ew.com/article/1995/04/07/chatty-kathy/ |access-date=30 March 2022 |magazine=Entertainment Weekly |date=7 April 1995 |language=en |archive-date=March 30, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220330045102/https://ew.com/article/1995/04/07/chatty-kathy/ |url-status=dead }}
*{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=975}}</ref> Several collections of film clips were shown throughout the broadcast highlighting various aspects of comedy such as troupes and dialogue.<ref>
*{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|pp=978–984}}
*{{cite news |last1=Archerd |first1=Army |title=Oscars plan to ‘Make ’em Laugh’ |url=https://variety.com/1995/voices/columns/oscars-plan-to-make-em-laugh-1117862661/ |access-date=February 22, 2015 |work=Variety |date=March 13, 1995}}</ref>

Several other people were also involved with the production of the ceremony. [[Bill Conti]] served as musical director and conductor for the event.<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=79}}</ref> Production designer Roy Christopher designed a new stage for the ceremony which prominently featured a [[proscenium]] which was designed to resemble the iris of a camera.<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=967}}</ref> Moreover, Christopher commented that the iris motif was inspired by the [[iris shot]] prominently featured in several comedic films and shorts.<ref name="Comedy Oscars" /> Dancer Debbie Allen choreographed ''[[The Lion King]]'' musical number.<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=76}}</ref> Actors [[Alec Baldwin]], [[Jack Lemmon]], [[Steve Martin]], and [[Rosie O'Donnell]] participated in a pre-taped comedic sketch lampooning auditions for a role in ''[[Cabin Boy]]'', the film in which Letterman made his film acting debut.<ref name="Wiley 1996 982">{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=982}}</ref>

===Box office performance of nominees===
At the time of the nominations announcement on February 14, the combined gross of the five Best Picture nominees at the US box office was $468 million, with an average of $93.6 million per film.<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars>{{cite news|title=1994 Academy Award Nominations and Winner for Best Picture |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1994&p=.htm |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=[[Box Office Mojo]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140705111722/http://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1994&p=.htm |archive-date=July 5, 2014 }}</ref> ''Forrest Gump'' was the highest earner among the Best Picture nominees with $300 million in domestic box office receipts. The film was followed by ''Pulp Fiction'' ($76 million), ''Four Weddings and a Funeral'' ($52 million), ''Quiz Show'' ($21 million) and ''The Shawshank Redemption'' ($16 million).<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars/>

Of the top 50 grossing movies of the year, 44 nominations went to 14 films on the list. Only ''Forrest Gump'' (2nd), ''The Client'' (12th), ''Pulp Fiction'' (14th), ''Four Weddings and a Funeral'' (20th), and ''Nell'' (41st) were nominated for directing, acting, screenwriting, or Best Picture. The other top 50 box office hits that earned nominations were ''The Lion King'' (1st), ''True Lies'' (3rd), ''Clear and Present Danger'' (6th), ''Speed'' (7th), ''The Mask'' (8th), ''Interview with the Vampire'' (10th), ''Maverick'' (11th), ''Legends of the Fall'' (27th) and ''Little Women'' (31st).<ref>{{cite news|title=1989 Box Office Grosses (as of February 13, 1995) |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/yearly/chart/?asof=1995-02-13&view=releasedate&view2=domestic&yr=1994&sort=gross&order=DESC&p=.htm |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=Box Office Mojo |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714221100/http://boxofficemojo.com/yearly/chart/?asof=1995-02-13&view=releasedate&view2=domestic&yr=1994&sort=gross&order=DESC&p=.htm |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref>

===Critical reception===
The show received a negative reception from most media publications. John J. O'Connor of ''[[The New York Times]]'' wrote, "Instead of keeping things moving smartly, Mr. Letterman stuck with his late-night shtick, too often leaving the show's pacing in shambles." He also added, "Within the show's first half-hour, with no strong hand at the helm, the audience simply sagged. Applause died long before most winners even reached the podium."<ref>{{cite news|last1=O'Connor |first1=John J |title=Critic's Notebook: The Winner Isn't David Letterman |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/03/29/movies/critic-s-notebook-the-winner-isn-t-david-letterman.html |work=The New York Times  |date=March 29, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130308120555/http://www.nytimes.com/1995/03/29/movies/critic-s-notebook-the-winner-isn-t-david-letterman.html |archive-date=March 8, 2013}}</ref> Television critic John Carman of the ''[[San Francisco Chronicle]]'' commented, "Last night on ABC, no one got it. Hollywood's big event was wonderfully littered by technical errors, bad taste, low comedy and lower necklines." Moreover, he remarked, "Letterman, the rookie host, was off his game in his opening monologue. Maybe it was the big auditorium. Or a billion people in the television audience."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Carman |first1=John |title=Telecast Was A Delicious Mess |url=http://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Telecast-Was-A-Delicious-Mess-3038891.php |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=San Francisco Chronicle |date=March 28, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714145004/http://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Telecast-Was-A-Delicious-Mess-3038891.php |archive-date=July 14, 2014}}</ref> Film critic [[Andrew Sarris]] of ''[[The New York Observer]]'' quipped, "Not only was he not witty or funny, he never knew when to let bad enough alone." He concluded, "As the evening dragged on, it became obvious that Mr. Letterman had no gift for ad-libbing through the few unpredictable opportunities in a 'live' event like the Oscars."<ref>{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=991}}</ref>

Some media outlets received the broadcast more positively. Television critic Joyce Millman of ''[[The San Francisco Examiner]]'' noted, "In his first stint as host of the Oscar telecast, David Letterman did the impossible—he made something entertaining from what is traditionally the most boring three hours of TV this side of a [[testcard|test pattern]]."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Millman |first1=Joyce |title=Late Show' star makes it fun |url=http://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Late-Show-star-makes-it-fun-3149651.php |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=The San Francisco Examiner  |date=March 28, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714220913/http://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Late-Show-star-makes-it-fun-3149651.php |archive-date=July 14, 2014}}</ref> ''[[The Buffalo News]]'' columnist Alan Pergament praised Letterman's performance as host writing "David Letterman was a box full of chocolates on an Oscar night that was empty of much emotion until the expected ''Forrest Gump'' sweep in the final 15 minutes." He also added that despite a lack of surprises amongst the awards, the emotional and unexpected humorous moments provided depth and entertainment throughout the evening.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Pergament|first1=Alan|title=Best Thing About TV Oscarcast was Letterman's Biting Humour|work=The Buffalo News|publisher=Berkshire Hathaway|date=March 28, 1995}}</ref> Hal Boedeker of the ''[[Orlando Sentinel]]'' gave an average review of the ceremony but singled out Letterman noting that he "proved Monday night that he's among Oscar's Top 10 Hosts. He's definitely at the top of the list with Johnny Carson, Billy Crystal and [[Bob Hope]]."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Boedeker |first1=Hal |title=After Slow Start, Letterman Brings Oscars To Life |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1995/03/28/after-slow-start-letterman-brings-oscars-to-life/ |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=Orlando Sentinel  |date=March 28, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714190437/http://articles.orlandosentinel.com/1995-03-28/news/9503280212_1_letterman-arthur-hiller-paul-newman |archive-date=July 14, 2014}}</ref>

===Ratings and reception===
The American telecast on ABC drew an average of 48.28 million people over its length, which was a 7% increase from the [[66th Academy Awards|previous year's ceremony]].<ref name="Oscar ratings">{{cite news |last=Gorman |first=Bill |title=Academy Awards Show Ratings |url=http://tvbythenumbers.zap2it.com/2009/02/17/academy-awards-show-ratings/12818/ |access-date=September 5, 2013 |work=[[TV by the Numbers]] |publisher=[[Tribune Company]] |date=February 17, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131109025135/http://tvbythenumbers.zap2it.com/2009/02/17/academy-awards-show-ratings/12818/ |archive-date=November 9, 2013 }}</ref><ref name="LA">{{cite news|last=Johnson |first=Greg |title=Call It the Glamour Bowl |url=https://articles.latimes.com/1999/mar/18/business/fi-18458/2 |access-date=August 26, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times  |date=March 18, 1999 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130928053918/http://articles.latimes.com/1999/mar/18/business/fi-18458/2 |archive-date=September 28, 2013 }}</ref> An estimated 81 million total viewers watched all or part of the awards.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Rickey |first1=Carey |title=A Miscast Oscar Emcee? No Best-host Prize For Letterman |url=http://articles.philly.com/1995-03-29/news/25701033_1_ed-sullivan-theater-letterman-fan-david-letterman |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=The Philadelphia Inquirer  |date=March 29, 1995 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714233250/http://articles.philly.com/1995-03-29/news/25701033_1_ed-sullivan-theater-letterman-fan-david-letterman |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref> The show also drew higher [[Nielsen ratings]] compared to the previous ceremony with 32.5% of households watching over a 53 share.<ref name=LA/><ref name="TVB Oscars">{{cite news|title=Academy Awards ratings |work=[[Television Bureau of Advertising]] |url=http://www.tvb.org/media/file/Academy_Awards.pdf |access-date=June 27, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130515152338/http://www.tvb.org/media/file/Academy_Awards.pdf |archive-date=May 15, 2013 }}</ref> It also drew a higher 18–49 demographic rating with a 21.7 rating among viewers in that demographic.<ref name="TVB Oscars"/> It was the most watched Oscars telecast since the [[55th Academy Awards|55th ceremony]] held in 1983.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Braxton |first1=Greg |title=One Day Later, Bouquets and Bricks for Dave : Letterman draws praise and criticism for his Oscar role, which helped show to its best rating in 12 years. But will the 'Late Show' star return next year? |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1995-03-29-ca-48291-story.html |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times  |date=March 29, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140715023433/http://articles.latimes.com/1995-03-29/entertainment/ca-48291_1_late-show |archive-date=July 15, 2014 }}</ref>

In July 1995, the ceremony presentation received six nominations at the [[47th Primetime Emmy Awards|47th Primetime Emmys]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Primetime Emmy Award database |url=http://www.emmys.com/shows/67th-annual-academy-awards |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=[[Academy of Television Arts and Sciences]] |publisher=ATAS |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714170525/http://www.emmys.com/shows/67th-annual-academy-awards |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref> Two months later, the ceremony won one of those nominations for Jeff Margolis's direction of the telecast.<ref>{{cite news|title=Who Won What: The Winners on TV's Annual Weekend of Awards |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1995-09-11-ca-44596-story.html |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times  |date=September 11, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131212125827/http://articles.latimes.com/1995-09-11/entertainment/ca-44596_1_comedy-series |archive-date=December 12, 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=1995 Emmy Award Winners |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/09/12/arts/1995-emmy-award-winners.html |access-date=December 29, 2014 |work=The New York Times  |date=September 12, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150203004055/http://www.nytimes.com/1995/09/12/arts/1995-emmy-award-winners.html |archive-date=February 3, 2015 }}</ref>
